And then explanations followed on paper signed by David Tolbert, who is now the Deputy Prosecutor and was at that time the Deputy Registrar, saying that my party had garnered a lot of seats in the parliament at the elections. Therefore, it was in the best interests of preserving the peace that they should try and prevent me from having any influence in future negotiations on who would be elected to form part of the government. This is on paper and the whole thing lasted for seven months. How should I now be expected to trust a registry acting like that? Or, for example, last year they accept this request from the OTP to cut off my phone again, to freeze my accounts, and to cut me off from my family. My cousin died and my son-in-law died, and I had no contact with my family just based on the suspicion that I had mentioned a protected witness, and I was only mentioning the name of whom I had previously and formally heard that he had testified in other cases for the OTP. And I told members of my party in Novi Sad, they are in peri-Novi Sad, which is the capital of the province of Vojvodina in Serbia to cut all their links with him because the previous pro-Western government had enlisted his assistance on building up certain facilities. The OTP never told me that he would be a witness in my trial to begin with, so that gave rise to this severe discrimination. Special measures were imposed on visits by my wife because purportedly I had given away names of protected witnesses to her, although up to that point in time I had not found out about a single protected witness name. It was only at a later stage that they disclosed to me seven or eight names of such protected witnesses, which I never shared with anybody else but my legal advisors. None of those protected witnesses can possibly complain that I tried to use my influence and affect them in any way through my associates. After all of what happened, I can hardly trust the registry to have any good intentions. On the penultimate day of my hunger strike, Hans Holthuis guaranteed to me, in writing, that I would receive all the documents on paper and in the Serbian language. One month later he tells me there was a misunderstanding. I was not authorised to provide any such guaranties on behalf of the OTP, he says. What sort of registrar is that and how can I possibly trust him? Whatever he -- guaranties he offers in the future, I will just laugh in his face -- which he lost for me. He lost face and he lost all credibility by that single action. You know, there are people in this Tribunal, Judges, Prosecutors, members of the registry, they come from their own jurisdictions. They often came across criminals and people who were just uneducated thugs. They think they can apply the same principles here, but they can't. The time is long gone when criminals appear before this Tribunal. That was at the beginning of the Tribunal's work. The people appearing now are the most prominent people, the most prominent Serbs, also belonging to other countries involved in this war, but most of the accused that stand trial here are Serbs, between 70 and 80 per cent. The most prominent Serbs from the 1990s are appearing before this Tribunal. Well respected Serb citizens and you simply can't afford to treat us like this. Some may agree to go along with that. I for one never will. I felt the need to provide this detailed explanation about my mistrust of the officials of the registry, which doesn't mean that I will refuse future contacts with them. I will never refuse any contacts. If there is something important to be discussed, I will ask for the conversation to be taped and to have the transcript later on. This is something that I did once and they did eventually submit to me a transcript in Serbian. That was in the autumn of last year sometime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, for providing your explanation regarding the mistrust you have with regard to the registry and you explained why. I shall have no comment on the merits, but personally speaking I must convey to you that the Detention Unit, as it functions, is under the competence of the warden of the Detention Unit and the Registrar and they both are entitled to have your conversations tapped. But there must be good reasons for that, reasons connected to security issues. I don't think you want to escape from the Detention Unit, otherwise it would be hard to understand why you surrendered to the Tribunal in the first place. I shall be very clear with you, Mr. Seselj. In my eyes, you are presumed innocent. You have all your rights, your civic and civil rights. The only difference there is between you and a person who would be outside, free, is that you are in detention because this Tribunal is seated in The Hague and because you have been indicted. This is the reason for your detention. But the fact that you are in detention must allow you to use your rights, certain rights, and when I found out that, during the election campaign of your party, you had been restricted in your rights, I was very surprised. That's all I can say to you on this point. Regarding your associates, you said that Ms. Regus is qualified and that her situation should be looked again by the Registrar. With regard to the equality of arms principle, the Prosecution, too, have a case manager and at the very least one could expect is that your case manager should have the same pay as the Prosecution case manager. There should be no dual standards here. I don't know what the salary is of an OTP case manager, but I shall look into this and I will not allow any discrimination in this respect, rest assured. But it's true to say that the case manager is a person whose qualifications, whose university qualifications, is rather low. It is not expected of a case manager that they should be graduated from university. There may be a solution for Ms. Regus. Please think it over. If this person became the interface between you and the registry, your own liaison officer, that might be a solution. In a way, if you look at a work contract, that could be a possibility, which I am going to review with the registry. I shall see how we could arrive at a solution. Indeed, gradually, I realise that this is an issue which might be a major hindrance to the smooth unfolding of our trial proceedings. So I shall endeavour to solve this problem, the problem of legal advisors, of Ms. Regus, of payment as quickly as possible. It may be that the Trial Chamber could issue a ruling if the obstacles are such that we have to issue a decision with regard to the rights of the Defence. I also wanted to deal with the issue of confidentiality. You and your Defence expert team have been filing requests which have been registered with the registry and I agree with you when you mention a name it is impossible for you to know initially whether the person you mention is a protected witness or not. And there is a real problem here that calls for some accurate explanations by me to you. You must know, Mr. Seselj, that the Rules allow the Prosecutor to file ex parte applications; that is, applications that only concern the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber without the accused being informed thereof. Let me give you an example. Under the Rules, it is allowed for the Prosecutor to ask the Trial Chamber for leave to disclose to the -- disclose to the accused the name of a witness and their statement only one month before the said witness comes to testify. In other words, I did not count them all, but it could be that the Prosecution -- Prosecutor has a number of witnesses whose existence you're not aware of. You will only learn the names of the witnesses and the contents of their statements one month before they appear to testify. Let's take a case. Imagine the Prosecutor wants to call a witness, say, in February 2008. Under the Rules, you will learn of the witness only in January 2008, that is, one month prior to their testimony. It may be that the witness is in a list or in a motion that you are going to file so that his name may be mentioned therein. So there could be like a -- some overlapping there, but I have no solution right now to this contradiction, as it were. With regard to the proceedings, you can have various types of requests or applications. You have public applications that are registered straight away by the registry and everybody can access them. There may be requests that are confidential ones. In such a case, the person filing the request must write in it that it is a confidential request. Let's take a theoretical case. Let us assume that you want to have a medical examination in hospital in The Hague, but there is a problem. You then file a request, but you do not feel the need in doing so of telling the public opinion that you're going to have an X-ray, for example. So you entitle your request "confidential request." Any confidential element is not disclosed to the public. Parties are also free to file requests that are ex parte requests. You, too, have that possibility. You can address a request to the Trial Chamber without the Prosecution being aware of it, but you then have to say it and you have to entitle your request "ex parte request," and vice versa. There can also be requests of motions that are confidential for the other party; that is, a motion that can be notified to the other party, but part of the motion that could be an annex will be ex parte. So it's quite complicated, you see. So together with your legal advisors, with Zoran Krasic, for instance, you have to look into all this, so that we're not faced with problems later on. So this is for the time being what had been decided and this is now what I'm going to change. What had been decided was that when you were going to file a motion in your own language, the motion was not recorded by the registry. It was turned over to the translation service and it was recorded by the registry only after it had been translated into English. So there is a bit of a shift in time, a time lag. And there is really a danger, in my view, inherent to this. If -- let's imagine you file a motion in your own language to explain a given topic to the Trial Chamber, you could speak about your health condition which calls for some medical intervention and it goes to translation and it remains there for several days on end, whilst your motion is an urgent one and needs to be acted on immediately. From now on, all motions filed by you will be recorded with the registry and will be passed on to the translation service. Once the document has been translated, it will be turned over to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution. But I believe it is fundamental when you file a motion, in keeping with the proceedings, it must be recorded. I know why this decision had been made, but I think we have to turn over that page and move on because initially there had been motions which could have been regarded as frivolous, and a number of your motions were not recorded. You gave us a lengthy explanation on this issue. You said why you had behaved in the way you had. Now we move on. This is behind us. You have a new Trial Chamber, you have a new Prosecution team, and we've spent a number of hours over the last three Status Conferences. And I never felt attacked/assaulted by what you said. What you said did not prompt me to react in any way. I fail to see why I should be concerned regarding your motions. But in this respect, I'll ask you for an explanation on two points so that this good atmosphere which is now setting in may develop as positively as possible. Mr. Seselj, I've noticed that sometimes when you speak, you speak quite loudly. Has it always been like that since you were a child, or is this due to the fact that you are in a courtroom and that you want to speak loud and strong? Could you tell me whether the volume of your voice is connected to this atmosphere of the courtroom or are you used to speaking like this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, perhaps you're not familiar with this, I was a university professor. I am used to expressing myself loud and clear. Secondly, I'm a professional politician. I spoke at countless rallies. Perhaps this is an occupational risk in a way in my line of work. Two of your colleagues from the Trial Chamber were also on the Milosevic trial where I appeared as a witness. Sometimes they had trouble dealing with the volume of my voice, sometimes it's a technical problem. We should have a technician lowering the volume if the perception of my voice is that it is too loud. I'm sure this problem can be resolved in a technical way. That is certainly not my intention. That's one thing that I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is what I thought, but you just said so. Secondly, and then we'll finish on this issue. On several occasions, I noticed that you do not address me as "Judge Antonetti" but "Mr. Antonetti." As a rule in all jurisdictions, Judges are addressed not with their names but with their titles: Mr. President, Your Honour, and so on. I know that Mr. Milosevic addressed the Presiding Judge of the Chamber with his name, but personally I'd rather you said "Your Honour." But if you insist on using my name, as you wish. I could call you "Mr. Professor" or "Mr. Seselj," just as you wish. But please clarify this for me. Why do you use my surname? Why don't you say "Your Honour"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, I'm addressing you by your name with no intention whatsoever of offending you. I have had extremely unpleasant experiences with previous Pre-Trial Judges. If you look at the transcripts, you can see that at the outset I addressed the first and the second Pre-Trial Judges as "Mr. President," but in the English transcript -- or "Mr. Judge." In the English transcript, it says "Your Honours." In the Serbian language and in our tradition, this has negative connotations, connotations of submissiveness, even connotations of sycophancy. It is quite unpleasant. People from my country laugh when they look at the videos of trials here where people address the Judges as "Their Honours." Even if our literary tradition, this habit has been ridiculed and is considered to be below human dignity. I have absolutely nothing against addressing you as "Mr. Judge" but only as long as we can have the very same wording in the English transcript without making me seem submissive, a sycophant or ironic for that matter. For as long as you run this trial in a proper way, Mr. Judge, you will have no inconvenience whatsoever from me. You can rest assured of that. If you want me to continue to address you like that, please deal with the transcript. I don't want that phrase in the transcript again, "Your Honours." I don't want to see that again. The former President of the Republika Srpska, Biljana Plavsic, was indicted before this Tribunal and the first morning she appeared here, she said "Good morning, Your Honours," and for years the Serbian public ridiculed her for that. That's how pathetic it sounded, believe me. We need to ensure that there's an accurate interpretation. As to how you address me, please just make it respectful. I have so many qualifications that I'm not much flattered by any used or not. What I really prefer is my family name, and that is what I'm really proud of. I see no problem with that. It is certainly also my desire that you do not take my address to you the wrong way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Seselj. Thank you, and I had understood it properly, you had no evil intention with regard to me. I tried to fulfil my mission which is to be a totally impartial --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll say it again. Mr. Seselj, thank you for what you said. I take due note of the fact that there is no bad intention towards me, and I'm all the more moved since I, as a Judge, do try to fulfil my mission for impartiality respecting all and sundry. I just wanted to put it out in the open so that this problem is solved once for all. Because for the last three Status Conferences, as I said, the climate is excellent, and I hope it will remain so in the future. Let us proceed. I'm now turning to the Prosecution because under the principle of equality of arms, the Prosecution, too, must do their job, must be able to work as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. If I may, there is one thing that I would like to address briefly, and that is the rest of what you have just said about protective measures. If memory serves me - and I don't have the documents on me right now - eight times the OTP requested protective measures in relation to certain witnesses, and the Trial Chamber, if I remember correctly, ruled that the names and other information should be disclosed to me a month before the beginning of trial and not a month before the testimony of the actual witness. Secondly, as far as ex parte documents submitted to you are concerned, I know that this is an entitlement of the parties to these proceedings based on the rules. However, whenever it is necessary for me to file a motion, prior to your ruling, it would be meaningless to file any such motions ex parte. For example, the OTP can submit something to you ex parte that is a matter of your internal communication between the Chamber and the OTP, something that doesn't affect my rights as an accused. If it's not something that has to do -- that has any bearing on my rights as an accused, then there's no need to do it ex parte. Secondly, the OTP are really pushing the envelope in all these witnesses requiring protective measures. I'm not sure if this has happened before, but it certainly is likely to happen at some point; for example, that my investigators get in touch with such and such a person, they talk to the person and ask the person to be a witness in my Defence case, and this person is already on the OTP list, possibly even a protected witness for the OTP, and we simply don't know it. It's a possibility. And that's what happens when the OTP start pushing the envelope in terms of protecting their witnesses. And then the witness finally comes along, appears in the courtroom, and all these protective measures are suddenly dropped. Finally, Mr. Judge, two years ago, I believe sometime in May or June, the OTP in full secrecy filed a motion to start proceedings against me for contempt of court. As far as I remember, you were part of that Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber ruled that the motion be dismissed. I still to this very day don't know what this was about. This was a Kafkaesque attempt to institute proceedings against me and for me to be tried for something, and I have no idea what this was about. When the whole thing was over, a court official informed me in a single sentence that the OTP had pressed for these proceedings to be started against me, and that the Trial Chamber dismissed this. I think I am fully entitled to know exactly why the motion was thrown out, particularly because according to the Rules, I was fully entitled before the Trial Chamber ever ruled to address the motion by the OTP. I think that my rights in that particular case were violated in a blatant manner. There are other problems surrounding the issue of protective measures. For example, there was this one witness, the OTP requested that the witness testify via videolink. I opposed this, their argument being the witness was ill, so they submitted this medical certificate about the witness's alleged illness, bearing no name of a medical institution, doctor, or an official stamp. At a Status Conference that I didn't attend, which took place during my hunger strike, the OTP claimed that they had simply cancelled out that information, erased that particular bit of information, in order to protect the secrecy and to protect the witness. They gave the name away, they disclosed the name to me, but they feel the need to protect the secrecy of the doctor and the medical institution, someplace or other in Croatia, that issued this certificate. It really is quite mind-bending, isn't it? Not to mention the fact that they claim someone is simply too old to travel here to testify; some people are afraid of flying; some people have stomach trouble; some people are suffering from pneumonia; all sorts of things like that. They are really pushing it too far with all these protective measures. Of course, when we have victims of rape or sex-related crimes, I do understand that fully. But if there is nothing to indicate that a witness is at risk, why just request protective measures for nothing? It is safer for a witness sometimes to have his name known, to have his name made public, than those kept secret. Nothing could ever clear my name if anything happened to a witness who was known to be supposed to appear in my trial and testify against me and if it suddenly became known that I had done something against this witness. So if all these names are kept secret, of course a certain degree of unpleasantness may occur every now and then, but that doesn't necessarily mean that I'm responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will now turn to the Prosecution, but I'll also answer what you've just said concerning protection measures. Indeed, the Chamber is seized of several motions concerning protection measures. I want to let you know immediately, Mr. Seselj, and also I want to tell the Prosecution what my position is for the moment in the managing of these motions. As I told you during the first hearing, I discovered by being a Pre-Trial Judge in this case there were a certain number of motions which were not yet answered, and I sorted out these several motions. I examined them one after the other, and there are two categories of motions. The first category which is going to need decisions of the Chamber for which I am the Pre-Trial Judge and which have to do with protection measures concerning several witnesses. In the coming days, decisions will be rendered. And there's another category of motions which is in stand-by, as they say in English, for which I consider that it would be appropriate for the Chamber - I'm talking about the Trial Chamber - to rule because those are motions which have to do with the substance of the case file. For example, the question of admitting your -- your own deposition in the Milosevic case. That has to do with the substance of the case, and I cannot myself with the Judges of the Trial Chamber III take a position while the two other colleagues who will have to judge with me might have different views. Therefore, there are a certain number of motions which, because they have to do with the substance of the case, have to do with the merits of the case, are of the competence of the Trial Chamber itself. There are also motions which are -- I would call them technical in such a way that -- and I say protection measures. Those can be decided upon as from now. I listened to you carefully and I intended, actually, to review the two motions concerning video conferences for witnesses who would be either ill or aged, too old, to come. I have seen your pleadings in this matter. You were opposed to video conferences for these witnesses. You questioned at least for one of them the fact that there was no medical certificate issued and, in particular, you argue that a video conference would not enable to cross-examine that witness. I have had -- I have seen in other trials a practice of video conferences, and it's true that between a video conference and the fact of having the witness here, it's preferable to have the witness present. But the video conference has also an advantage which is to enable certain witnesses to -- not to have to travel by air because of their state of health and so on. So the Chamber has to check whether these conditions are true before allowing a videolink. But you have to know, Mr. Seselj, that nevertheless when there is a videolink, the accused may counter-examine -- cross-examine without any problem. There is practically no technical difficulty because this happens in a realtime, and you can see on the monitor the witness, and this procedure of the videolink is satisfactory generally. But in the two cases you have indicated, I will check in-depth to see whether it is true that it is impossible for these two witnesses to come in person. As you know, because of the age of certain persons, it may be difficult for them to travel. But all this has to be attested to by a medical certificate. Therefore, on these two matters I'm going to review the matter in-depth. I also noted that, as a principle, you are against protection measures. This is what you have described in your pleadings. You know that protection measures exist in other countries, and a Tribunal has defined the procedure by Rule 75. So there are -- there is some leeway where the Chamber may have and other cases in which we have absolutely no leeway. It's the case of witnesses who have already had protection measures in other cases. For instance, let's us imagine that a witness may have been a witness in the Milosevic case with protection measures. The protection measures in question which was granted to this witness will have the same effect for a witness in your case. On there, I can strictly do nothing. The Chamber is tied -- has its hands tied by the measures decided by the other one. Now, in which case do we grant protection measures? We grant protection measures when the witness has objective reasons, perhaps in certain cases also subjective reasons, to fear for himself or his family because of bearing witness because of his deposition. So this, of course, is reviewed and is examined, and it is true that, for instance, if a politician is called as a witness and requests protection measures, one can be surprised, because normally it is a person who presents himself in public, and therefore I don't see why he wouldn't do so in front of court. There are other people - and I see that you actually opposed this and this surprised me - that was about victims in the case of a sexual assault which requests protection measures so that their own tragedy be not known, either by their own family, because sometimes the members of the family don't know anything about it, or even the neighbours. And in that case, the Chamber grants the request in the interest of the victim who doesn't want what has happened to him or her be known outside the courtroom. You have this type of witness which, as a rule, will be granted these protection measures. Where the Chamber decides on protection measures, it -- it is always motivated, reasoned, with good reason, it's not just by chance. You have a request from the Prosecution, there's an answer of the accused, and the Judge rules either in favour or against the request or against the motion. Now, Mr. Seselj, you have to know also that yourself, when you will call your own witnesses, I don't know who your witnesses will be, but it's possible that some witnesses who will want to come here, speak in your favour, may say, Yes, I agree to do so, but I need protection measures. And therefore, you yourself may be led to ask for protection measures for the witnesses. The history of this Tribunal is very telling. In all the cases which have been touched here, there have been protection measures in favour of Prosecution witnesses but also in favour of the witnesses of the accused, protective measures. This is what I wanted to tell you in general concerning protective measures which, of course, need to be reviewed case by case. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, I really don't know what kind of interpretation you received, but I fully agreed as far as victims of sex crimes were concerned that protective measures were needed. Perhaps the interpretation you received said the opposite. I, as a legal man, truly justify that, and in my country if protective measures are applied, then it is in family law, marital relations, and with a view to victims of sex-related crimes. At first, I did not oppose motions of the Prosecution for protective measures. You can see that from the case file. I started opposing that only when it was my assessment that the OTP had really overdone this. Testifying by videolink, introduce protective measures, is indeed envisaged by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; however, the Rules clearly show that this can be done only in exceptional cases because otherwise the principle of public trials is infringed upon. The tendency enforced by the OTP is that this should turn into customary practice. Very soon testifying without protective measures is going to be the exception rather than the rule. Before you know it, videolink is going to be the rule, too. I know from other cases, the accused told me and their lawyers did, too, that sometimes it happened that videolink witnesses had a prompter in front of them who would prompt the kind of answer that they were supposed to give, or another person altogether would appear and testify in the name of the said person, an actor would appear, and so on and so forth. Not to go into the question of intelligence services, the Muslim service, the Croat service, and many others that were involved in preparing false witnesses. That is why I insist that in the future as well this should be an exception. There is also the principle of hearing direct testimony and having a public trial. These are very important principles. Judge, you are trying me, you and your colleagues are trying me, but the public is judging you. These are two parallel processes, and they cannot evolve without -- one cannot evolve without the other. That is why closed sessions have to be the exception rather than the rule and with strict control as well. The number of protected witnesses has to be brought down to a minimum, and testimony by videolink should be allowed when one sees that for objective reasons anything else would be impossible rather than having things done the way OTP is used to having them done. Since you raised a very important issue, I would like to present yet another problem. At the last Status Conference, part of our hearing was in closed session. If you look at the transcript, you will see there was no need to go into closed session then. From May last year onwards at some other Status Conferences, again a few times we would go into closed session, and it was obvious that there was no reason for going into closed session. I think that whenever a request is made to move into closed session, that very strong reasons have to be presented for that, and I have the right to challenge those reasons. And then it is the Trial Chamber that decides whether closed session is required not, not like in some other cases and other hearings where they are more often in closed session than in public session. Since you mentioned the Slobodan Milosevic case, what happened was that the witness did not ask for protective measures at all - this is Dragan Vasiljkovic - and the protective measures were dropped immediately. He walked into the courtroom and said, I never asked for this. And there was a few others. Aleksandar Vasiljevic came as a protected witness and then he testified in public; Zoran Lilic, too. I'm just talking about what the public knows and what was disclosed. I'm not going into the other things that remained a conspiracy. There are some absurd situations and without any reason for that. For me, it is of vital importance to have public testimony heard. This is of paramount importance because it is only in that case there is a point to a trial. If the main part of a trial is going to take place in closed session with protected witnesses, why have a trial at all? Protected witnesses can send their statements, and you can phone me and tell me what your judgement is, and that's it. The point of a public trial is that the public judges the Trial Chamber. Any judgement, even when it becomes final, can be criticised, can be challenged by legal scholars. And for this scholarly public to be able to criticise the Trial Chamber, the Prosecutor, the content of the judgement, and so on and so forth, they have to have maximum information made available to them. That is why I'm not asking you to rule out these two provisions of the Rules in totality, but I'm just saying that they should be applied only to a minimum, a minimum that is justified by very strong arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have noted what you have said. It is true that during the last hearing I requested a closed session because, if I remember, there were some motions from the Prosecution which were confidential and which concerned certain protected witnesses. Therefore, to be sure, [indiscernible] I preferred to go to closed session so that the name of the witness would not be disclosed in a public hearing. This was the reason why I had requested passage to closed session. But you will see that today, it is not the case. I am now addressing Prosecution, and I want to ask the Prosecution within the framework of the preparing of this case, which I am trying -- in which I'm trying to solve all the problems which we have or the obstacles, it would be fit for the Prosecution, on the one hand concerning the list of the witnesses and exhibits of Rule 65 ter, check that the witness list is, indeed, a list which is up-to-date because there is some pressure concerning certain crime places. All this has to be up-to-date. So please check that the list of witnesses is up-to-date. As for the list of exhibits for the Prosecution, the 2.827 exhibits, I have faced the following problem which I had explained to you last time. These 2.827 exhibits are not put in chronological order. Just as Mr. Seselj, I work on documents after document, one by one, and when there is a problem, I take my binder and I look at the document. And when the documents are in chronological order, it's easier to see where one stands. Would it be possible for you - it shouldn't be too complicated - to review the 2.827 documents and place them in sequence, in chronological order, with number 1 being the oldest document and number 2.827 being the most recent document. Perhaps, I don't know, 1994, 1995, and number 1 as being the first one. So present your list differently. And once this will have been done, put an extra column where you would indicate for each document the dates when the document was transmitted or disclosed to Mr. Seselj. For instance, let's take document number 1, I don't know what document it is, but document number 1. This document was transmitted to Mr. Seselj in English and in his language at what date, so that I won't at a given moment discover that there are some documents which have not been transmitted or disclosed. Of course it means a lot of work, but this work will enable you to re-position properly these documents chronologically and also to check thoroughly that there hasn't been any mistake concerning the disclosure of the documents in question. Because in certain cases this could have certain consequences, repercussions. I know that there is one column, the first one, with the figures, the numbers of the documents; the second one is a description of the documents; the third gives the date; the fourth is the ERN number in English for the -- the next one is the ERN number for the B/C/S versions; and the following is the type of document, whether it's a video or whatever; and finally, the name of the witness with which and through which the exhibit will be presented. So there has to be a column added to that which will indicate the date at which the document or exhibit was transmitted or disclosed to the accused. It would have been also a good idea to add one more column, if it's feasible according to the means you have at hand, to add one more which would indicate document by document the references to the paragraphs of the indictment. This document corresponds to which paragraph of the indictment? For instance, just at random, as I see it the document 2.231 is a photograph. The date is unknown. Normally this photograph should be put through a witness VS026. So the extra column would say at what moment the photograph in question was transmitted to Mr. Seselj and the other one would say that this photograph refers to this or that paragraph of the indictment, which would then be extremely useful for the handling of the documents. There is also the pre-trial brief, and I have heard what you yourself have indicated, Mr. Seselj, and after that I will stop this hearing because I have this afternoon another hearing. I have another case which I have to preside upon this afternoon. So, Mr. Seselj, I would call to your attention in particular the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution which has to be reformatted according to the new events which have happened, the crime places, the reference to document -- the redaction of the number of crimes, and all this translated into your own language. You will have, yourself, the possibility to answer in writing, and this may need a certain time. We are here in the system, it is very different from what you may have done in your own country because when the Judges rule within their deliberations at the end of the trial, they rule on the basis of the indictment, on the pre-trial brief which is a form of indictment, a very developed indictment, and also on the basis of witness statements during the trial, during the trial, during the -- during the -- during the cross-examinations and the pleadings, the arguments, and within this framework the Judges will have to examine closely the pre-trial brief as well as the answers given by the accused to the arguments of the pre-trial brief. Therefore, this shows the interests for an accused to answer to the pre-trial brief because this pre-trial brief touches upon legal questions, factual questions, and the fundamental question of the responsibility of the accused. And if the accused does not answer, says nothing, there is a sort of imbalance in what is called the equality of arms. I know that when this trial started you were having a hunger strike and you refused to answer, and so on, but since we are re-starting on a new basis, I ask you very specifically to pay attention to the need to answer to this pre-trial brief because your written answer will, in fact, be the essentials of your defence. And this will be a very useful instrument, very useful tool. I'm not asking you to take a position now, but I want to be very aware about this question which is fundamental, fundamental because the pre-trial brief supports the indictment and there's a development, a detailed development, of the arguments of the Prosecution. All the more so as the pre-trial brief, as I say just by memory, there are about 3.000 documents, but the pre-trial brief refers to 500 documents which are mentioned, which means that yourself, in your filings, you may criticise the references made to the 500 documents in question and also the arguments presented. I also call your attention to the fact that the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution begins by a chapter concerning your role as a leader of propaganda in Greater Serbia and all the details are given after that. Therefore, from there, your interest is to answer in writing to this, although if you don't answer this, I can't oblige you to do so. But as a Judge, I have the duty when I see that there is an imbalance between one side and the other to try and re-establish balance so that no prejudice is suffered. This is what I really wanted to tell you, and I'm now asking the Prosecution to reformat, as I said, the pre-trial brief and the documents, but today I cannot give a date for the beginning of the trial because of the number of problems which have not been solved and which are obstacles, serious obstacles, to the beginning of this case, and in particular the case of disclosure or communication of documents in hard copy and in the language of the accused as well, of course, as the question of the help the accused needs with the legal assistants and so on. So we have to conclude now. Mr. Seselj, do you want to have the floor on something? We will of course meet again in about a fortnight or three weeks. And I will also give you the floor, for the Prosecution. Yes. So, Mr. Seselj, would you like to say something on another subject before we close this session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wish to inform you that I would be very interested in responding to the pre-trial brief, but the last time the OTP filed a pre-trial brief I faced an enormous number of references that the OTP invoked in their footnotes, whereas I did not have the documents available to me at the time. These references were related to rulings in other trials, often having to do with interlocutory appeals. Those in reference to judgements were easier for me to deal with because I received copies for those for the most part, although the OTP were behind with that, too. Next they invoked judgements made by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and I simply don't have the references. That is why, Mr. Judge, I would like you to rule that the OTP submit to me all the references that they invoke in addition to their pre-trial brief. If they can't deal with that, they should reduce the number of references, of things that they reference in their footnotes. In order to be able to respond, I should have the references in my possession, I don't and therefore I can't. The OTP don't seem to have that. They should be translated into Serbian. Many of them are in Serbian, but I think the registry should be ordered to submit that to me. The last time I filed a motion written by hand in which I enumerated all the documents invoked by the OTP in their pre-trial brief that were not available to me. This is a very serious problem. Also, Mr. Judge, I would like you to hand me a deadline for this response to the pre-trial brief, and if I could have a month for that. This is somewhat longer than is usual for a deadline like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will have a month, but starting as of the time when the pre-trial brief is finalised with references to documents in chronological order, and it must be made sure that the pre-trial brief has been updated factoring in the amended indictment. And once this document has been prepared, it will be recorded, and that's the time when the one-month deadline will start. But it is one month as of the time when that document will have been translated into B/C/S. It has to be in B/C/S for the accused to be able to respond to it. In conclusion, I'm turning to the Prosecution, if they want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly I have three questions. You changed the procedure regarding the Registrar filing Mr. Seselj's submissions prior to the translation, and I wanted to clarify. My understanding is that the calculation of time for response would be triggered by the translation rather than the filing in Mr. Seselj's language. The second is that we will be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Absolutely. It will be starting as of the time when the translation is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The second is I wanted to bring up the fact that the Appeals Chamber in the Brdjanin case issued a relevant decision regarding the theory of liability that applies to this case in joint criminal enterprise. It's important that that judgement be translated with all deliberate speed to make it available to Mr. Seselj. We are reviewing the indictment as well as the pre-trial brief to confirm that we are fully within the law as enunciated by the Appeals Chamber. This is a matter that we had foreshadowed in our pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this didn't escape me because, as you know, in the Brdjanin case, the Appeals Chamber had to look into this matter, into the issue of joint criminal enterprise, and it is of course in the interest of Mr. Seselj to know, to be made aware, of the Brdjanin appeals decision in his own language. I shall ask the translation service to tell us when they will be able to convey to you the Appeals Chamber judgement, but the Prosecution, too, will have to see whether there's need to change anything in the indictment or in the pre-trial brief following the recent case law, and that Brdjanin appeals decision of course goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We will undertake to review the suggestions to improve the information contained in our exhibit list and continue to report back to you. Our hope is that the case is ready for trial in November of this year, and we'd like to work toward that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are telling us that you are working towards the date of November 2007. Mr. Seselj has heard this date just the same as I did. I will do everything I can personally so that we can start as early as possible, but everybody will understand that there is a series of hurdles to get over. I pledged to see you every two to three weeks. As soon as I know when the next Status Conference is going to take place, we shall convene a hearing. I will report to you the outcome of my meetings with the Registrar, see whether we could make some headway on certain issues and also to tackle other issues which I haven't yet had an opportunity to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Very briefly, it occurs to me also that the disposition of the pending motions relating to the method of reception of evidence will greatly assist us in finalising trial preparations, including giving the Chambers information regarding the method of testimony and exhibits. So to the extent that the pending motions are now at issue with Mr. Seselj having responded, we would appreciate a ruling on them as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl, I listened to Mr. Seselj with care earlier on when he said he really wished to meet with the OTP as long as they wanted to meet with him. Mr. Seselj explained to us that he sees no problem in that, provided he be assisted by his associates, by the people working with him. I think this is where the hurdle is, and it really is minor. So please, talk about this to Ms. Carla del Ponte, tell her that the Pre-Trial Judge has taken due note of the fact that the accused is willing to meet with the OTP, but in order to do so he wants to be assisted by his associates, by the people he works with, to prepare for trial, which seems to me to be quite an acceptable claim.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We're very willing to consider whatever suggestions he has regarding meeting and to listen carefully to the suggestions that he might propose and consider those as part of the pre-trial process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The time has come to adjourn. Thank you. Thank you to all the people who helped us during the hearing. We shall meet again shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: adjourned at 12.43 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24
